articles.title: Congress snubbed delimitation talks: Government signals Parliament session
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Days after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge called for an all-party meeting to discuss any fresh delimitation proposal, govt on Monday
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Days after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge called for an all-party meeting to discuss any fresh delimitation proposal, govt on Monday said it had already consulted many opposition parties, including Samajwadi Party, DMK and NCP (SP), and could not hold talks with Congress because of its own unwillingness, refuelling the buzz that Parliament may be called for a short duration to take up the legislation.In a sharp response to Kharge's Oct 16 letter to PM Narendra Modi, parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said, "When after repeated requests Congress didn't give dates for discussion, govt's outreach extended to other political parties. Consultations were held with representatives of parties including SP, DMK, YSRCP, NCP (SP), Shiv Sena (UBT), AIMIM and BJD with a view to building a broader consensus in support of the proposed legislation."In these circumstances, it was not clear why the demand for consultation was being made repeatedly, he added, rejecting Kharge's suggestion. Rijiju sought to give the impression of Congress's isolation over the issue by emphasising govt's consultations with other key members of the opposition in contrast to both Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, not giving him any date for discussion when he had met them during the last session.Writing to Modi, Kharge had also questioned the "unprecedented" delay in proroguing the monsoon session, which was adjourned indefinitely on Aug 13. Dismissing his contention, Rijiju cited precedents and underlined that no constitutional requirement existed prescribing a specific period within which a House must be prorogued following its adjournment sine die."The mere fact that a House has not been prorogued does not, by itself, give rise to any constitutional or procedural impropriety or irregularity," Rijiju said. — Kumar RakeshGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Egyptian parliament delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Lawmakers adjourn session as opposition party tells members to abstain over unclear commitment.
articles.body:
Egypt’s parliament has delayed a vote on authorising its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia, which has come under increasing attack from the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen.

The vote has been adjourned to October 26, the House of Representatives said on Monday. The move prolongs the debate over Egypt’s role in the Yemeni conflict.

The opposition Egyptian Social Democratic Party said it had told its lawmakers to abstain.

The party said parliament had not been given enough information about the mission’s objectives, duration, cost, or the risks to Egyptian troops.

However, the party, which holds nearly a dozen seats, said most of its lawmakers support the measure, according to two members of parliament who spoke to the AFP news agency.

The parliament has been tasked with authorising President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to approve any request from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance amid attacks on the kingdom by Yemen’s Houthis.

The call for support came after the Iran-backed rebel group attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco last week. Saudi authorities say 13 people were killed in the October 10 attack on the airport.

El-Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take “any measure” needed to protect its Gulf allies.

“I’m not talking about confronting or attacking anyone,” el-Sisi said. “We’re talking only about defence.”

After approval from the National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, Egypt’s constitution requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority to send troops on a combat mission abroad. The council gave its approval on Sunday.

The Grand Imam of al-Azhar urged Arab and Muslim leaders on Sunday to mediate Egypt’s parliamentary decision and avert further bloodshed.

Saudi Arabia holds an important role in financing Egypt’s rocky economy. It is due to deposit $5.3bn into Egypt’s central bank this month, plus $267.39m in interest.

Egypt’s EGX30 stock index fell early on Monday amid concerns about possible military involvement but recovered to close 0.4 percent higher.

Nematallah Choucri, head of research at HC Securities, told the Reuters news agency that geopolitical developments are the main driver of recent market losses.

Egypt is also affected by the shortage of oil and gas exports from the Middle East due to the United States war on Iran and fighting in Yemen.

Egypt’s economy is heavily dependent on remittances from Egyptians working in the hydrocarbons industry in Saudi Arabia.

Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to Saudi Arabia also threatens the Suez Canal , which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the Houthis launched attacks in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in solidarity with Gaza in 2023.

James also said Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom”.

Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact with Riyadh, signed in August, amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.

articles.title: 'The View' co-hosts defend El-Sayed comparing himself to JFK over Muslim Brotherhood scrutiny
articles.summary: "The View" co-hosts clashed over whether Abdul El-Sayed's family's alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood are a legitimate concern or Islamophobic questioning.
articles.body: "The View" co-hosts defended Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his comparison of questions about his family's alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood to scrutiny former President John F. Kennedy faced over his Catholic faith. El-Sayed made the comparison during an "MS NOW Reports" interview on Saturday, likening questions about his family's alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood to scrutiny Kennedy faced over his Catholic faith. Co-host Whoopi Goldberg highlighted an incident at a recent town hall when El-Sayed was asked whether he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed did so, but objected to the question, saying the audience member was "implicitly assuming that I’ll have dual loyalties." "I liked what he said. He compared the question he received to John F. Kennedy's question because John F. Kennedy, as you know, was a Catholic, and in the days he was running that was a huge deal and people wanted to know ‘Are you going to listen to the Pope? Are you going to listen to the people?’" Goldberg said. CONTROVERSY OVER ABDUL EL-SAYED'S FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD IGNORED, DOWNPLAYED BY LIBERAL MEDIA "Yeah, because he was the first Catholic president," co-host Sunny Hostin agreed. "And I loved that comparison because, when John F. Kennedy was asked, he said, ‘I am not running to be a Catholic president, I'm running to be president who happens to be Catholic.’ And candidate El-Sayed said the same thing. ‘I am running to be a senator who happens to be Muslim.’" "I think he does politics extremely well," she continued. "And there has been these constant Islamophobic — these Islamophobic comments around his candidacy. Trump called him a jihadist. I mean, this is just, I think it's out of line. I think it's out of pocket for our country to be a country where all religions aren't welcome. I think that it's really despicable the way he's been treated." Concerns about El-Sayed's family's alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood emerged after social media posts uncovered by the Washington Free Beacon showed El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, described her family's history with the organization. In one 2012 post, Abdelhadi described a conversation with her and El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, about her involvement with the organization during college in Egypt, saying, "Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college #respect." MICHIGAN DEM AG TURNS ON EL-SAYED OVER TERROR ATTACK RESPONSE, WARNS OF MENTALITY THAT 'BOTHERS ME A LOT' Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin noted how quickly El-Sayed disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, but said she was still troubled by his response to an antisemitic terror attack in Michigan, arguing that such concerns cannot be disregarded as "Islamophobic." She also pointed to his past campaigning with far-left streamer Hasan Piker. Fellow co-host Sara Haines argued, "The comparison to JFK isn't quite an equitable comparison, because when you question his loyalty based on his Catholicism, that's different than asking a question about reported ties to a terrorist organization." She added that while the reported ties involved El-Sayed's family, not El-Sayed himself, the fact that people were framing concern about the Muslim Brotherhood as Islamophobia was making the entire conversation worse. Co-host Ana Navarro argued that concerns about the Muslim Brotherhood were overblown. "The Muslim Brotherhood is practically defunct in Egypt. That's like asking him to denounce bell-bottoms," she said. "To me, this is a binary choice. Do I want somebody that's going to push back on Trump or do I want someone that's gonna rubber-stamp Trump?" Navarro asked. "Well, I want something that's going to demand accountability, that is going to demand oversight, and that's to pushback on the abuses of power that are going on in this country by this administration right now." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Human rights attorney Brooke Goldstein, executive director of The Lawfare Project and founder of the #EndJewHatred movement, spoke to Fox News Digital about the segment and criticized Navarro for downplaying the Muslim Brotherhood. "Nobody asked El-Sayed about his faith," Goldstein said. "He was asked about the Muslim Brotherhood, whose Egyptian and Jordanian chapters were designated as foreign terrorist entities by the Treasury Department this year for materially supporting Hamas, and whose Lebanese chapter was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the State Department. Hamas even describes itself as the Brotherhood’s wing — and clearly neither the Brotherhood nor Hamas is 'defunct.'" "The question El-Sayed deflected — the comparison to Kennedy is inapt because Kennedy actually did answer the question, to a room full of Protestant ministers — is about national security concerns, not religious ones," she continued. "The Kennedy comparison is nothing more than a deflection from unanswered questions about a designated terrorist organization." "The co-hosts of ‘The View’ are missing the point," Goldstein added. "JFK faced religious prejudice. Questions about Abdul El-Sayed’s alleged family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood raise a different concern: where does a candidate’s loyalty lie, with the United States and its constitutional values, or with a foreign terrorist organization?" "The evidence cited to raise these concerns is compelling enough to warrant serious scrutiny and direct answers," she said. "Voters have every right to demand transparency when potential connections to Islamist movements are questioned. National security is not bigotry, and invoking discrimination should not end legitimate debate." "Anytime there’s serious questions into somebody’s affiliation with a terrorist group, they claim religious prejudice," Goldstein continued. "Asking somebody about their ties to a terrorist organization is anti-Islam, what then, is pro-Islam?" "Meanwhile, DSA candidates are advancing an anti-Western ideological agenda that deserves far more scrutiny. Their radical socialist policies and hostility toward traditional American values risk weakening the institutions and freedoms that made this country exceptional," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Goldstein cited rioting in France as an example of what can happen if such issues aren't taken seriously. "France is a warning of what can happen when progressive ideology, failed integration policies, and inadequate responses to Islamist extremism collide," she said. "America must not follow that path by handing power to DSA radicals who put ideology ahead of national interests."

articles.title: How do we support ketamine users when their needs are so different?
articles.summary: For the last two years Megan has been in agony and unable to stand straight because of her ketamine use.
articles.body:
Megan Harmes was 14 when she first tried ketamine.

A decade later, rehab is helping her rebuild her life after bladder issues caused by the drug have left her needing to wear incontinence pads.

The drugs charity Kaleidoscope says it has seen a huge rise in referrals to its detox and rehabilitation facility over the last five years, with two people referred in 2021 compared to 112 so far this year. The majority of clients are aged 18 to 24.

Research is now underway by the University of South Wales into the specific needs of this group, as the harm caused by "chronic, escalating use" of ketamine is far more rapid, over a shorter space of time, than from alcohol or Class A drugs.

Services traditionally designed for older adults are having to adapt to support much younger people, it said, with very different needs, with habits often formed while they were in school.

For 24-year-old Megan, from Flint in north Wales, drug use became more common among her peers during lockdown.

As an aeronautical engineering apprentice, she was suddenly working from home, on full pay, with access to a drug whose price had plummeted.

She said at its worst, she was on it "all day, every day", as according to Megan it helped to suppress symptoms or feelings associated with ADHD and borderline personality disorder.

"I'm very hyperactive now that I'm sober. I haven't been like that since I was 14, it suppressed pretty much everything," she said.

Eventually her ketamine use meant she lost her apprenticeship, causing her to "spiral".

Megan later found work elsewhere, but four years of night shifts further entrenched her use, as she would use ketamine to stay awake through the night even on days off.

For the last two years she has been in agony, unable to stand straight and needing to wear incontinence pads.

"For a 22-year-old wearing pads or nappies, it takes away all dignity," she said.

"Back then I really didn't care whether I lived or died - now I don't want to die.

"I've been in rehab just over four weeks and I'm getting back to my old self."

Megan said she wouldn't know the extent of the damage to her bladder for some time, but she has put on weight and is physically feeling better than when she arrived.

Jo Moore runs the Birchwood rehabilitation facility for Kaleidoscope and said five years ago they had just one referral for inpatient detox from ketamine.

"Since January this year we've seen 112 people come through the door," she said, adding that half their clients are currently being supported for ketamine use.

"It's very, very cheap and very accessible - that's what allows people to use it more frequently and at large amounts at the same time."

The drug is prescribed in healthcare settings as a dissociative anaesthetic, and also used with animals, but was reclassified as a Class B drug in 2014. This means it is illegal to take, carry, make or sell.

Illicit ketamine use among those aged between 16 and 59 in the UK was estimated to be about 264,000 people in 2024-25, with those seeking treatment for ketamine use disorders increasing twelvefold over the course of a decade.

While younger people have driven the rise in its use, Moore said the last year had seen a rise in referrals for adults aged 25 to 34, particularly in Cardiff and south-east Wales.

Dr Darren Quelch, from the University of South Wales, said interviews with service users at Birchwood suggested use started from as young as 13.

He said the physical harm caused by persistent use ranged from memory problems and chronic pain to bladder damage and kidney failure, but that support services were having to rapidly adapt as the needs of users are more complex.

"Their bread and butter isn't dealing with really complex medical presentations," he said. "Even if they were, we actually don't know what the right answer is yet."

He is now conducting research alongside Kaleidoscope to establish what types of support work for this specific patient group.

"The population is inherently different to lots of other groups that might engage with drug and alcohol treatment services," he said.

Mark said his health had deteriorated to such an extent that "at the age of 25 I probably had the body of an 80-year-old".

"I was no longer functioning like a proper human being," he said.

As a keen footballer growing up in Liverpool, he now looks on jealously at others his age, walking without pain.

"It stopped me being a father to the little girl that I've got - I stopped being the big brother, the responsible son," he said.

Mark would regularly pass clots and experience pain during urination, but said the collapse of his nose from snorting drugs has had a huge impact.

"It completely destroys self-confidence - which leads to more drugs, because that just blanked out what I think of myself."

It's one of the reasons he has asked to remain anonymous.

"I started getting looks of disgust from my own family, which destroyed me. It was a very lonely time through my addiction," he said.

Mark's drug use started at 18, but by 21 he said he was using "copious amounts of cocaine and ketamine".

He initially sought help from his GP in Liverpool, but was too ashamed to admit he was using ketamine for fear of being dismissed or judged.

It's an issue reflected in Quelch's research. He found young people struggled with A&E and GP surgeries, as their symptoms weren't always linked with ketamine use, or the question wasn't always asked.

"That's not necessarily because people aren't asking the right question, but we don't actually know what works well at the moment," he said.

"There's very little provision for young people experiencing drug and alcohol-related harms, and that has almost left us starting right from the beginning."

Moore said things were improving, with greater availability of early intervention in the community, reducing the need for detox.

"We're seeing less people presenting to services with a new substance use of ketamine - so the education in schools, colleges and universities is actually working.

"But we are seeing an increase in people that have been using for a couple of years that we are going to continue to have to help and support."

With trends in drug use evolving, Moore said the challenge for both the third sector and the NHS was to adapt around the needs of clients, but that the involvement of those with lived experience had made a difference.

"I can see improvements now, but there have been some really difficult times where it felt like we were shouting in the dark."

Quelch said while research continued, the scale of the current ketamine problem was still unclear, as was the longer-term health implications.

"Anecdotally, relapse is a big problem in this group - we don't know the recoverability of their bodies, but we have seen that when people resume using ketamine after a period of abstinence, those harms appear a lot quicker than the first time around," he said.

However, Quelch added the work being done with peer support at Kaleidoscope was "really unique and impactful".

"There was a lack of judgement or stigmatisation - the peer element was really important and is something to learn from the Birchwood environment."

For Mark it has meant a focus on the future is possible. Like many we spoke to, he was adamant he wanted to give something back.

"I grew up thinking money was everything, but I get joy now from helping other people who are struggling. I was there once and I know how much it means to get someone to help you."

articles.title: Texas’ oldest pari-mutuel horse racetrack closed in 2010 after 35 years; 16 years later, its roughly 150-acre Manor Downs site could become a 1 million-sq-ft industrial building as locals ask to save its history
articles.summary: According to KXAN, the Austin Business Journal and records from the Texas Comptroller, a former Texas horse racing venue that once hosted music
articles.body: According to KXAN, the Austin Business Journal and records from the Texas Comptroller, a former Texas horse racing venue that once hosted music performances and major community events could be transformed into a large industrial development, reviving a long-delayed redevelopment plan while raising concerns about the loss of a local landmark. More than a decade after its closure, the site remains largely undeveloped. Now, Dallas-based Dalfen Industrial is preparing to move forward with a revised proposal that could bring a building measuring approximately one million square feet to the property.According to KXAN’s October 17 report, Manor’s economic development director, Scott Jones, said the developer’s original industrial park concept had shifted towards a speculative building, which would be constructed before a tenant had been secured. A formal development plan had not yet been submitted to the city at the time of the report. The proposal could become one of Manor’s largest development projects, although the final design, construction schedule and overall cost remain unclear.A long-delayed redevelopment planDalfen Industrial purchased the property in 2021, with plans for an industrial park reported by the Austin Business Journal. The city of Manor annexed the land in 2022, but construction had not progressed as initially anticipated.Changing market conditions and higher borrowing costs have contributed to the delay, according to city officials. A Texas Comptroller database entry provides further details about the development agreement involving DG Manor Downs Property Owner, L.P. The agreement, effective April 2, 2025, runs until April 2, 2038, subject to its termination provisions.The agreement describes plans for at least four buildings totalling 894,650 square feet, with an option for two additional buildings adding another 487,944 square feet. The anticipated total construction cost is approximately $100.56 million. The agreement also lists a maximum monetary value of approximately $14.6 million. It identifies real property taxes and wastewater impact fees among the sources associated with the agreement.These figures describe the broader development agreement and its potential build-out, rather than confirming the final cost or specifications of the latest proposal. The city had not yet received the updated development plan described in KXAN’s report.Residents want the site’s history preservedFor some Manor residents, the proposed redevelopment is about more than the future of a large tract of land. It also raises questions about what happens to a venue that formed part of the community’s cultural and family history. Ruth Biscoe, 78, recalled spending weekends at the racetrack with her family, where her father sold barbecue chicken. The deteriorating buildings remain a reminder of those years, and she hopes the property can retain a place where families can gather.Another local resident, Robert Battaile, has argued that the community’s identity should be considered alongside the economic benefits of redevelopment. He has advocated for preserving the area’s character rather than allowing industrial development to become its defining feature. The concerns reflect a broader tension facing growing communities around Austin: industrial projects can generate taxable property value and support economic development, but they can also replace places with long-standing local significance.Proposed park and amphitheatre could offer a compromiseThe revised proposal reportedly includes a plan for the developer to donate nine acres to the city. Jones expects the land could accommodate park space and an amphitheatre, potentially creating a public destination that acknowledges Manor Downs’ musical history. However, the precise design and use of the proposed public space have yet to be confirmed, and the city is still awaiting the development plan. KXAN reported that Dalfen Industrial had been contacted for comment but had not responded by the time its story was published.For now, Manor Downs stands between two possible futures: a major industrial project that could expand the city’s tax base, and a community effort to preserve the memories associated with a venue that operated for 35 years. articles.title: Saudis postpone investment conference until 2027 amid fighting with Houthis
articles.summary: The Saudi government has postponed its annual investment conference — known colloquially as “Davos in the Desert” — to next year, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels carried out multiple deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia earlier this month. Organizers at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute postponed the 10th edition of the conference, which was set…
articles.body:
The Saudi government has postponed its annual investment conference — known colloquially as “Davos in the Desert” — to next year, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels carried out multiple deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia earlier this month.

Organizers at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute postponed the 10th edition of the conference, which was set for Oct. 26-29 in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.

“This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers, and delegates,” Dr. Maha bint Mishari Al Saud, the CEO of the FII Institute, said in a statement .

“Because this is our landmark tenth edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves,” she added.

Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, said her institute will announce “new dates” for the postponed conference “soon.”

The list of speakers for the event included Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the governor of the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia; Meta President Dina Powell McCormick; JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon; BlackRock CEO Larry Fink; and Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon.

The conference’s “Davos in the Desert” moniker is a reference to the annual World Economic Forum’s annual gathering in Davos, Switzerland. It is part of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s push to transition his country’s economy away from oil and toward Western investment, tourism and sports.

The Houthis, who have fought a Saudi-led coalition in the decade-plus Yemeni civil war, recently ramped up their attacks on the kingdom .

A pair of Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed at least 13 people and injured at least 320 others, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation .

The Iran-backed rebel group also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have stated that airports are legitimate targets in their conflict against the Middle Eastern nation.

President Trump said Friday that the Saudi government would be receptive to support of the Israeli government in its fight against the Houthis.

“Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel’s support and our support,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

articles.title: An Oregon woman was working three jobs to keep up with her mortgage; when the family’s heating system failed, they received a $16,000 replacement for free
articles.summary: Diane and Brian Johnsen, a retired couple from Beaverton, Oregon, can now face the winter in comfort after receiving a new HVAC system worth $16,000 at no
articles.body: Diane and Brian Johnsen, a retired couple from Beaverton, Oregon, can now face the winter in comfort after receiving a new HVAC system worth $16,000 at no cost. “We were ecstatic,” Brian told KOIN-TV as the couple received the unexpected gift through the Lennox Feel the Love programme.Answer to their prayersThe Beaverton couple were stretched thin. Diane took on three jobs to keep up with the mortgage on their home in Beaverton, Oregon. Money was tight, and every bill counted. And that’s when the heating and cooling system stopped being worth repairing. A technician could not get it working again at a price that made sense, so the couple faced a bigger problem. They needed a new system, and they had little room in their budget to buy one.That’s when they turned to the Lennox Feel the Love programme. It is a community initiative that helps qualifying homeowners get essential home improvements at no cost. Lennox donates the equipment, and local dealers install it for free. The programme is built on that partnership between the manufacturer and the people who work on the ground.The Johnsens hoped that the programme would help them, and it did. They received a complete heating and cooling system and a new thermostat. The equipment was valued at about $16,000. Aviator Heating & Cooling, a local contractor, handled the on-site installation.When they heard the news, the couple couldn’t hold back. “Are you kidding? We were ecstatic,” Brian told the broadcaster.Feel the love programSince 2009, more than 3,100 recipients have received new systems through Feel the Love, Lennox says. In 2025, the company said it had donated 402 units that year alone. Those numbers cover homeowners and non-profits across North America.Aviator says it wants to help families in need across Beaverton, Portland and the surrounding communities in Oregon and south-east Washington. The company’s work for the Johnsens fits that goal.For the Beaverton couple, this is nothing short of a blessing. For people of retirement age, a reliable furnace is more than a comfort. It is a question of safety and peace of mind through the coldest months. Diane put it simply: “Especially in our retirement years, it means the world to us.”Diane and Brian Johnsen’s story has drawn attention well beyond Beaverton, and the Feel the Love programme is getting much of the credit. Since 2009, Lennox has donated heating and cooling systems to families in need, and local dealers install them for free. The arrangement is simple, and that may be part of why it works. For one retired couple, a system that could not be repaired is now one that will keep their home comfortable for years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zelensky rolls the dice on combative Trump pressure campaign
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is making a high-stakes bet that a combative public pressure campaign targeting President Trump — in coordination with his allies in Congress — will push the president to reverse course on concessions to Russia. Zelensky, under intense strain from relentless Russian strikes and depleted air defenses, has lashed out at Trump…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is making a high-stakes bet that a combative public pressure campaign targeting President Trump — in coordination with his allies in Congress — will push the president to reverse course on concessions to Russia.

Zelensky, under intense strain from relentless Russian strikes and depleted air defenses, has lashed out at Trump for offering to buy Russian diesel and waiving sanctions meant to throttle resources for Russia’s war machine.

So far, Trump has responded by ramping up his criticism of the Ukrainian leader — repeating demands for elections in Ukraine, calling Zelensky the main obstacle to peace and downplaying Russian attacks on the country.

Even some of Zelensky’s backers in Congress don’t see the wisdom in his approach.

Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), in a text message to The Hill, said Zelensky has been cautioned against lashing out at Trump “as it will not end well.”

Some observers note Zelensky has pulled back from some of his harshest criticism immediately following the announcement of a deal for the U.S. to buy diesel from Russia. At that time, Zelensky called Trump “weak.”

McCaul participated in a Zoom call with Zelensky earlier Monday, along with other lawmakers, and said the Ukrainian leader “did not say anything negative” about Trump.

Zelensky has also pointed his finger at the U.S. government for restricting Ukraine’s ability to use satellite communications Starlink and Starshield, run by tech billionaire and close Trump ally Elon Musk. Trump has said that neither he nor Musk called for a slowdown.

Zelensky has avoided assigning specific blame but again told NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday: “Of course the message came from [the U.S.] government, I don’t know from whom or what Cabinet.”

McCaul is among a handful of Republicans urging Trump to withdraw a waiver he issued Friday suspending sanctions meant to economically isolate Russia, authorized by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act which was signed into law last month.

But McCaul, who is leaving Congress, has not gone as far as Republican Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (Pa.) and Don Bacon (Neb.), who have committed to blocking Trump’s agenda if he doesn’t change course on Ukraine.

“I’m trying to be more constructive,” McCaul told The Hill.

The number of Republican defections spurred by Trump’s actions on Ukraine are increasing but “not enough,” said John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine and senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center.

While intense criticism against Trump could cause him to back off pressuring Ukraine in the short term, the president has repeatedly returned to Putin-friendly positions in his efforts to end the war. Herbst pointed to Trump abandoning last year a 28-point peace plan proposal in the face of widespread pushback but said some of those ideas — calls for Zelensky to cede territory in eastern Ukraine to Russia or release frozen Russian assets — reappear at different times.

He also pointed to Republican lawmakers seeking to walk a tightrope between supporting Ukraine and the president.

Rep. Mike Turner (Ohio) is one of those Republicans. Speaking with Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday, he joined calls for an investigation into who limited Ukraine’s access to Musk’s satellites. But he stopped short of endorsing the more hard-line approach of some House colleagues.

“I don’t think there’s any brinksmanship that needs to have to occur on this,” he told Brennan.

Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) — who visited Zelensky in Kyiv last week — said he expects Trump’s waiver on the Graham sanctions bill to be a “short-term pause.”

Cramer said he backed a proposal by Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, for the U.S. to give Ukraine targeting information on Russian launch sites in exchange for Kyiv halting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

“I would hope we can get to that point where, remembering that what President Zelensky is protecting are civilians. Russia has chosen to go after civilian populations,” Cramer said Sunday on “Face the Nation.”

Zelensky on Monday detailed a “horrific” Russian strike on the Kharkiv region, where a 1-year-old girl was killed in her stroller, the mother later died in the hospital, and an 11-year-old child was killed. On Saturday and overnight to Sunday, Russia launched 337 drones and a ballistic missile, according to an analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

Russia over the past week launched nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 guided and other aerial bombs, and 66 missiles — most of them ballistic — against Ukraine, Denys Sienik, the Charge d’Affaires of the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, D.C., said in a statement to The Hill.

Sienik said Starlink and Starshield services still face restrictions.

“Ukraine’s position is guided not by a desire for confrontation, but by the fundamental responsibility to protect its people and preserve its ability to defend itself while pursuing a just and lasting peace,” Sienik continued.

“In the situation of Russia’s escalation, meaningful and sustained pressure on Russia remains essential to creating the conditions for genuine progress toward peace.”

Part of that pressure is Ukrainian attacks inside Russia, which have persisted despite Trump urging Zelensky to back off.

Ukraine launched a major attack on Russian oil refineries in St. Petersburg over the weekend — hitting an oil refinery, a cable-stayed bridge, a data center and electricity substation — which impacted electricity for about 20,000 civilians, the Institute for the Study of War noted.

Sienik said those attacks are reciprocal for Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure.

“Ukraine remains committed to pursuing peace and supports efforts to secure a ceasefire through talks with Russia,” he said.

“Any indication that continued aggression can yield strategic gains risks reinforcing the Kremlin’s conviction that its military approach can succeed.”

After nearly two years of mediation efforts, Trump and his top officials are increasingly convinced that Zelensky is the obstacle to peace, said Mark Episkopos, a research fellow in the Quincy Institute’s Eurasia Program.

“The territorial issue is the big one. Ukrainians have made clear no intention of withdrawing from Donetsk, this continues to be a hard Russian demand that I don’t see the Russians walking back on,” he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored that point in an interview Monday with the conservative news outlet Breitbart.

“This war is honestly about one part of Ukraine called Donetsk,” Rubio said.

“The core of this conflict is that Russia demands all of Donetsk, including that defensive line, as part of their territory. That’s what they have defined as victory. And Ukraine has said we can’t give up that 11 percent that’s remaining of Donetsk because that defensive line is our last defensible line. Hence, that is at the core of this conflict.”

Ukraine’s supporters — and Zelensky — argue Putin would not stop at taking Donetsk and that his ultimate goal is Ukraine’s complete subjugation.

Episkopos argued Zelensky is making a wrong bet that majority support from members of Congress and backing from Europe strengthens his hand with Trump. He said Kyiv risks graver U.S. pullback if it fails to engage constructively with the White House.

“Clearly Trump and Zelensky don’t get along, but this is much deeper,” he said.

“This is about people in the White House, and I think President Trump himself concluding that if there is no peace deal that can be reached in the foreseeable future, then it’s time to do what Trump, [Vice President] JD Vance, Marco Rubio, and others have been threatening for over a year, which is to slowly start walking away.”

articles.title: In 1971, Nike co-founder Phil Knight hired college student Carolyn Davidson to design the iconic Swoosh logo for $35; in 1983, he gifted her a gold Swoosh ring and 500 shares of Nike stock
articles.summary: Carolyn Davidson, the graphic design student who created Nike’s iconic Swoosh logo for just $35 in 1971, received a gold ring featuring the Swoosh and 500
articles.body: Carolyn Davidson, the graphic design student who created Nike’s iconic Swoosh logo for just $35 in 1971, received a gold ring featuring the Swoosh and 500 shares of Nike stock from co-founder Phil Knight in 1983.According to Portland State University, where Davidson studied graphic design and Knight taught accounting, she initially worked with Knight on charts and graphs before being asked to design a stripe for a new running shoe.How Carolyn Davidson met Phil KnightDavidson’s association with Nike began in 1971, when Knight was running Blue Ribbon Sports, an Oregon-based business that distributed Japanese Onitsuka Tiger running shoes in the United States. Knight and his business partner, University of Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman, were preparing to launch their own line of footwear and needed a distinctive logo.Davidson was a graphic design student at Portland State University. According to her recollection published by the university, Knight approached her after overhearing her talking about being unable to afford an oil painting class. He offered her design work, initially asking her to prepare charts and graphs for a presentation.The assignment eventually led to an opportunity to design a stripe for the company’s shoes. Knight wanted a mark that conveyed speed and looked different from competitors’ designs, including Adidas’ three stripes.Davidson sketched several possibilities on tissue paper and presented them to Knight and his team. The design ultimately selected was the curved, swooping mark now known as the Nike Swoosh. Knight was reportedly not immediately convinced, saying, “I don’t love it, but maybe it will grow on me.”Davidson billed him $35 for the design. She continued working with the growing company for several years before it began using outside advertising agencies.Phil Knight’s gift to Carolyn Davidson in 1983In 1983, Davidson was invited to meet Nike executives for lunch but arrived to find a reception organised in her honour.She received a gold ring shaped like the Swoosh and set with a diamond, along with 500 shares of Nike stock, recognising her contribution to the company’s visual identity.How Nike’s stock splits affected the original 500 sharesNike’s official records list seven two-for-one stock splits. However, the first took place in January 1983, before Davidson received her shares later that year. The six subsequent splits would have increased her original 500 shares to 32,000, assuming she retained the entire holding.Nike’s stock closed at $37.21 on October 19, 2026. At that price, 32,000 shares would have a theoretical value of approximately $1.19 million. This calculation assumes the original shares were retained through all six subsequent splits and does not establish Davidson’s current holdings.In an interview with ESPN, Davidson said she had sold some shares after the stock splits. articles.summary: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) revealed Monday that he would be speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about his country’s loss of access to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink internet, vowing to hold any U.S. officials who limited the application “fully accountable.” In a post to social media, Fitzpatrick said he would speak with…
articles.body:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) revealed Monday that he would be speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about his country’s loss of access to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink internet, vowing to hold any U.S. officials who limited the application “fully accountable.”

In a post to social media, Fitzpatrick said he would speak with Zelensky and his team later this week to discuss Starshield, President Trump’s recent decision to waive U.S. sanctions on Russia and other matters related to Ukraine’s defense.

“I will be assuring President Zelenskyy that anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head,” he wrote on social platform X .

Ukraine said Wednesday it was suddenly unable to use Starshield and that Starlink also had been affected, hindering its defense operations and ability to stop Russian attacks. Prior to the outage, the Trump administration had reportedly threatened to cut off intelligence and weapons support to Ukraine over Kyiv’s harsh criticism of Trump’s surprise deal to import Russian diesel.

Fitzpatrick last week called the slowdown of both Starshield and Starlink internet in Ukraine a “major problem,” saying that Congress would respond if the U.S. abandons its support for Kyiv.

Trump and Elon Musk, the owner of SpaceX, have both said that they did not cause an outage of Starlink and Starshield.

On Monday, Zelensky told a bipartisan group of U.S. senators that Ukraine still does not have full access to the satellite-based Starshield network or U.S. intelligence sharing.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who was on the call with Zelensky, said Democratic and Republican senators are preparing to act immediately to signal their displeasure that the administration hasn’t given Kyiv the same access to intelligence and internet connectivity — crucial to operating drones and other military vehicles — as it had at the start of October.

Ukraine also has accused Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of deliberately dragging his feet to approve the transfer of a vital batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for the country.

On Monday, Fitzpatrick said Congress “will unequivocally reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally to the United States, that Russia is a self-declared enemy of the United States, and that the United States will 100% support and defend the people of Ukraine in their fight for their own freedom against this brutal, illegal, and unprovoked Russian invasion.”

He called on the U.S. to provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself and said Washington “must not import a single drop of Russian oil.”

“Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they’ve ever been before,” he wrote. “Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor—and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.”

articles.title: Cause of death released for 3 who perished at Burning Man festival in Nevada
articles.summary: Three Burning Man 2026 deaths in Nevada's Black Rock Desert were linked to cardiovascular disease, methamphetamine, MDMA and cocaine toxicity, according to new reports.

articles.title: Mahmoud Khalil asks Supreme Court to let U.S. judges quickly reverse immigration detentions
articles.summary: Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let federal judges quickly determine the legality of immigration-related detentions so that people cannot be held for months or years without judicial oversight.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let federal judges quickly determine the legality of immigration-related detentions so that people cannot be held for months or years without judicial oversight. In papers filed with the high court, Khalil asked it to overturn a ruling earlier this year by the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia that found federal courts do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of the detentions until immigration courts had fully considered each case. Khalil, a lawful permanent U.S. resident, was detained by immigration authorities last year because of his participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations at Columbia University in the spring of 2024. The U.S. government argued at the time that Khalil’s presence in the U.S. was harmful to the country’s foreign policy interests. As a result, the former Columbia graduate student spent over three months in detention before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered him freed after finding that the federal government had acted unconstitutionally. Khalil told a remote news conference Monday that the appeal was “bigger than just my ability to stay here.” He said he wanted to ensure that thousands of immigrants, documented or not, can challenge the Trump administration's “unlawful” attempts to stop protected speech. He said the administration knows “all too well its baseless allegations and smears against me cannot survive the slightest scrutiny in federal courts,” so it wants to channel it into “kangaroo” immigration courts where it can control the outcome. In a statement Monday, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said: "It is a privilege to be granted a visa or green card to live and study in the United States of America. The Trump Administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority with respect to Khalil, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews, and damages property. We would encourage him to use the CBP Home app and self-deport.” The 3rd Circuit has put its ruling on hold so that Khalil could appeal to the Supreme Court. He remains free. Although the Supreme Court typically agrees to grant only a small percentage of appeals requests, the U.S. government has already asked the high court to overturn a federal appeals court decision that upheld a judge's decision to release Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri. That ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia, directly conflicted with the 3rd Circuit decision in the Khalil case. Sometimes, conflicting appeals court rulings can increase the chances that the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case. If it does, oral arguments before the justices would likely occur sometime next year.

articles.title: In pictures: Dussehra celebrated across India as a symbol of good over evil
articles.summary: The festival, which commemorates the triumph of good over evil, is celebrated with different rituals across India.
articles.body:
Millions of people across India are marking Dussehra, one of the country's most widely celebrated Hindu festivals, with processions, prayers and the ceremonial burning of giant effigies to symbolise the triumph of good over evil.

The festival is observed with different rituals and traditions across different parts of the country but with grand celebrations everywhere.

It commonly marks the deity Lord Ram's victory over the mythological 10-headed king Ravan.

The festival coincides with Vijayadashami, celebrated in eastern, southern and other parts of India, to honour goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

Hindus follow a lunar calendar, and Dussehra falls on the 10th day after Navratri, a nine-night festival of worship and celebrations.

In the days leading up to Dussehra in northern India, performers wear elaborate costumes and make-up to stage Ramlila, the dramatic retelling of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana. They recount Lord Ram's exile and his wife Sita's abduction by Ravan, culminating in the battle that symbolises the victory of good over evil. The final act is followed by the ritualistic burning of the effigies of Ravan, his brother, Kumbhkaran, and son Meghnath.

The vibrant stage is usually accompanied by a carnival-like atmosphere with food stalls, rides and smaller performances.

In the east and some other parts, as well as among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival sees devotees worshipping the divine feminine power with Durga Puja celebrations.

Temporary tents housing idols of Goddess Durga and other deities are set up across cities and towns. People visit these structures, known as pandals, where Durga is often depicted slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

Current affairs often make their way into the traditional celebrations, like theme-based decoration of tents in Kolkata city, which is famous for its Durga Puja celebrations.

Dussehra also marks the beginning of preparations for Diwali - the festival of lights - which is held 20 days later.

articles.title: Pimping websites: Human trafficking 'hidden in plain sight' online
articles.summary: A Stormont inquiry looked at four main websites that advertise women for sexual services across Northern Ireland.
articles.body:
Human trafficking is a "catastrophic" problem that is being "hidden in plain sight online", a Stormont inquiry has found.

The investigation into "pimping websites" in Northern Ireland was prompted by growing concerns about the exploitation of trafficked and vulnerable women on online platforms.

The All-Party Group (APG) on Human Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation is due to release its inquiry report on Tuesday.

The report said such sites allowed criminal gangs to manage multiple profiles and conceal abuse behind the pretence of the women being independent.

It said 95% of women and girls trafficked were "brought for the purpose of sexual exploitation".

The APG inquiry looked at four main websites that advertise women for sexual services across Northern Ireland - Locanto, Adult Works, Viva Street and Escort Ireland.

The websites are publicly available and people will select women and make contact usually through the website, WhatsApp or Telegram.

The women are listed as "independent escorts" offering an extensive list of services. However, the reality is much different, the report found.

Victim A was forced into prostitution at 19 and advertised online. She said the sites were not neutral platforms.

"They provide the infrastructure through which sexual exploitation can be organised, marketed and monetised," she said.

"You have the websites but they bring the people from online actively looking for girls, our customer base knew that we were either being drugged before the appointment so that we were completely incoherent, you could not say yes or no, your body is paralysed, that's not said online."

Another survivor was managed by a man who controlled the profiles of multiple women trafficked from Brazil.

"None of us had access to the emails from buyers. They came directly through him, he answered as if he was us."

The report also states the National Crime Agency has identified websites advertising prostitution as "significant enablers of trafficking and sexual exploitation".

BBC NI has spent months looking through these websites and, on average, there are more than 500 women advertising sexual services daily in Northern Ireland.

Many of the women are moved around, from city to city. For example, "Chloe" was advertised as being in Belfast for 24 hours.

The following day she was being advertised in Dublin with the same line "in the city for 24 hours". Over the next week, she was advertised across the island of Ireland in six different cities, always for 24 hours only.

Ruth Breslin, from the Sexual Exploitation Research and Policy Institute, said there were many cases before courts, "both in the Republic and in the north of Ireland where these sites have played a key role in the sexual exploitation and in the human trafficking of women in the sex trade".

"We know that women who have been exploited and trafficked are being advertised on these sites," she said.

"Banning these sites is the right way to go. Regulation just won't be strong enough in this space. Even if we regulate this space tightly, the exploitation would still continue."

The BBC contacted Escort Ireland for comment, but it did not respond.

It is the biggest site on the island of Ireland and has been in operation for 30 years.

It carries a disclaimer that "the charges are for time and companionship only", adding that "anything that occurs is a matter of coincidence and choice between consenting adults".

The report rejected the idea that the platforms can be safely regulated. It stressed that criminal networks would "continue to exploit regulated environments unless the digital infrastructure itself is dismantled".

It outlines some recommendations, including criminalising website operators, improving cross-border operational cooperation with the Republic of Ireland and targeted interventions for men.

Connie Egan is the deputy chair of Stormont's all party group on human trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation.

"We now owe it to every woman who is advertised in Belfast today and every girl trafficked across this island against her will to ensure this report is not just read, noted and shelved," she said.

"Hidden in plain sight across our country is the reality of sexual exploitation and all its associated harms and websites advertising prostitution are undeniably driving this.

"I hope survivors and those still trapped in prostitution will hear and read of our recommendations and recognise that they do have a voice."

The exchange of sexual services for money is legal in England, Scotland and Wales.

But legislation introduced in 2015 makes it a criminal offence in Northern Ireland to pay for sex, either directly or indirectly.

However, selling sexual services is not illegal, nor is loitering or soliciting to do so, but running a brothel or controlling prostitution for profit remains a criminal offence.

Since the legislation was introduced on 1 June 2015 to 28 February, there were 134 arrests for the offence for sexual services; of those arrests, 105 were referred to the PPS; five led to conviction.

Det Ch Supt Emma Neill, who heads the Police Service of Northern Ireland's organised crime branch, said: "Our clear focus is on identifying and safeguarding victims who have been exploited, while identifying and gathering evidence against members of organised crime groups involved in that exploitation.

"Our huge challenge is that sexual exploitation is often an unseen crime. It can happen in plain sight. It's a challenging issue, which cannot be solved by policing along and which requires collective efforts."

articles.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world
articles.summary: As the strongest El Niño on record continues to intensify, what impacts on weather patterns are already being felt across the globe? Sarah Keith-Lucas looks at the evidence.
articles.body:
El Niño has been strengthening for several months now and is already having a significant impact on global weather patterns.

Countries including Indonesia, India and the United States have been experiencing droughts, floods and heatwaves in line with projections about how extreme weather events will be supercharged by the phenomenon.

The World Meteorological Agency says the record-breaking El Niño will strengthen further and persist until at least 2027.

Here are five ways its impact is already being felt around the world.

Indonesia battles worst wildfire season since 2015

Indonesia, which typically trends drier and hotter in El Niño years, is battling its worst wildfire season since 2015.

This year, since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned.

This is more than twice the area burned last year without the influence of El Niño.

The wildfires have led to school closures and an increase in hospital admissions across Indonesia.

Millions of people in Sumatra and Kalimantan have been exposed to toxic haze from the fires and around 175,000 people have suffered from respiratory illness.

More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers.

East Pacific explodes with hurricane activity

In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far.

There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes.

This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.

Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.

Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.

The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño.

Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo.

Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month.

Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie.

Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.

Atlantic hurricane season remains eerily quiet

In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.

El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.

There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.

This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward).

Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.

In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point.

This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.

Reduced monsoon rain threatens agriculture in India

The drier and warmer theme has also taken hold in India, where the essential monsoon rainfall has been 13% below average.

While the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) would consider this still to be in the 'normal' range, the overall average doesn't reflect the variation in rainfall across India.

While Central India had around its normal expected rainfall, the east and north-east were around 26% drier than average and put into 'exceptional' drought. Southern states of India were 24% drier than average.

Even where rainfall was nearer to average, the rain did not fall continuously as is typical during the monsoon, instead flipping between long dry spells and extreme rainfall.

This adds more stress and vulnerability to agriculture yields.

India is influenced by a number of different weather patterns that can affect the monsoon season and so scientists suggest that El Niño may not have been the only factor.

Strong typhoons target east China and Japan

Further west in the Pacific, it's also been an active season in eastern China and Japan as storms including Maysak and Dujuan have brought recent widespread floods and landslides.

According to the Japanese Meteorological Agency, there have been 10 tropical cyclones forming in the western Pacific Ocean - the highest number in a season since 1966.

During El Niño the warmer Pacific brings changes to wind patterns, meaning cyclones tend to form further east, away from Japan and east China.

However, this means there is a bigger distance and more time where storms can feed off the warmer waters, gaining energy to become more intense typhoons before they hit land.

Scientists believe that additional typhoons are likely to develop this year with the potential for further impacts to Japan or east China.

articles.title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
articles.summary: Women share their experience of lichen sclerosus.
articles.body:
This report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms.

Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush.

Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain.

"I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says.

Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy.

She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms.

"Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says.

"But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad."

The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus.

The lifelong inflammatory condition affects genitals and can cause white patches to form with itching, soreness, splitting and tears, says Dr Nighat Arif, a GP specialising in women's health.

It affects men and women but is more common in women over 50 . There is also a small risk of vulval cancer.

"It's very sore to have sexual intercourse, to pass urine and it gets mixed up with sexually transmitted diseases but it's not contagious," she tells BBC Radio 5 Live podcast That Time of the Month .

Research into the prevalence of vulval lichen sclerosus is limited but analysis by the University of Bristol of people in the West Midlands and Warwickshire estimated it affects about 1% of women.

Dr Sophie Rees, who helped conduct the research, tells the BBC: "This is almost certainly an underestimate, as we know that there is often a very long delay to diagnosis, and some people probably go their entire lives undiagnosed.

"There is unfortunately a lot of shame and embarrassment around seeking help for vulval symptoms, as well as a lack of awareness, even amongst healthcare professionals."

She adds: "More research is badly needed into true prevalence."

Monica says multiple misdiagnoses had a "significant" impact on her mental health.

"I didn't know how to go on... with having no answer, it was just a horrific, lonely time."

She was given medication for herpes. "I was very upset in an appointment with a dermatologist who got quite angry with me because I was like, 'it's not that'.

"Then she said that she wanted me to have blood tests for HIV."

Doctors told her she was "too young" to have lichen sclerosus.

"But sadly, women do have it at all ages, you can have it as a child. So I found that really quite difficult, but I always knew that it wasn't right."

Monica believes there should be more support for those with lichen sclerosus.

"Once you have a diagnosis, you're still necessarily not treated in the manner that you should, I don't even get a checkup," she says.

"I manage it on my own with my steroid cream and hope that I'm doing everything right."

According to the NHS website, the cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown. It might be caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin.

It is not contagious, caused by an infection or by poor personal hygiene. Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger the condition or make it worse.

Clare Baumhaeur, 53, from Kent first experienced symptoms aged five.

"I was itchy and I was sore, and I was always told off, I wasn't obviously aware what was going on."

Her symptoms worsened into adulthood with tears, blisters and sores.

"But you don't see other vulvas, so I had no idea mine wasn't normal. I'd had in that time eight smear tests as well and nothing was ever said."

In 2016 Clare experienced a tear which did not heal.

"I was 43 that year, having it for 38 years at that point, I just couldn't take it any more."

A GP told Clare she had herpes and to go to a sexual health clinic, she says she was "shocked" as she had been married for 25 years.

She was eventually referred for a biopsy and was diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and vulval cancer.

"I'd never heard of lichen sclerosus and also I had a cancer that I'd ever heard of in a place I'd never heard of.

"That was the first time I heard the word vulva, no health professional had mentioned it, so it was a lot to take in at that time."

Clare had been in remission from vulval cancer for seven years, when a regular check-up revealed a cancer recurrence and she underwent surgery three years ago.

In June another check up found pre-cancerous cells and she had a sixth surgery.

Clare believes if she had been diagnosed with lichen sclerosis earlier, her cancer may have been diagnosed before it got to stage three.

"I had to have radiotherapy twice and that's left me with instant early menopause, lymphoedema and nerve damage."

Monica encourages women experiencing any changes to their body to keep a diary.

"It's really important that we get to know our bodies better, to know what's normal for you in your private parts as well, because actually our vulvas do change.

"If you are being dismissed, get multiple opinions, just keep going back because you don't have to live without answers."

She recommended the Lichen Sclerosus Guide which has a diagram and template to help you talk to doctors.

articles.title: Tehran rejects any role in plot to kill leaders of German Jewish groups
articles.summary: Tehran summons German envoy after two men convicted of trying to kill leaders of Jewish groups, rejects any role.
articles.body:
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned Germany’s ambassador after a court in Hamburg found two men guilty of plotting to kill two leaders of Jewish organisations at Tehran’s behest, accusing Berlin of leveling “baseless political allegations”.

The decision to summon envoy Axel Dittmann came after Germany summoned the Iranian ambassador, Majid Nili Ahmadabadi, on Monday over allegations that Tehran was behind the plot to assassinate the two pro-Israel public figures.

“Levelling security-related accusations against Iran has long been a tactic employed by the Zionist regime and certain Western nations,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement broadcast by official news agency IRNA.

“Attempting to provide a judicial face to baseless political claims not only fails to lend any credibility to such allegations but also undermines the standing of the German judiciary itself,” the statement added.

Berlin’s allegations stem from a court case involving two men, a Danish national and an Afghan national, who were convicted in a Hamburg court on Thursday for planning to target the president of Germany’s main group representing the Jewish community and the head of the German-Israeli society.

The German Foreign Ministry said on X that the Iranian ambassador had been summoned, adding Tehran would not be allowed to “threaten our free society”.

“The malicious assassination attempts against Josef Schuster and Volker Beck will have legal consequences,” it added.

“We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and on those who defend it anywhere, and certainly not in Germany.”

The Dane, partially identified as Ali Hassan S, was jailed for eight-and-a-half years. The Afghan, who was recruited as his accomplice, was sentenced to four-and-a-half years.

Iran’s intelligence service steered the two men, the court said. The pair were arrested in Denmark last year and extradited.

In sentencing the men, the judge said they were guilty of “terrorist activities orchestrated by Iran”.

At the time they were charged, the Iranian embassy in Berlin released a statement rejecting what it called “unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran’s enemies”.

articles.title: Criminals in hospital set to lose benefits under new rules
articles.summary: The families of the victims of Nottingham killer Valdo Calocane had been campaigning for the change.
articles.body:
Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.

Regulations due to be laid in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years while already having their bed and board funded through the NHS while receiving psychiatric treatment.

The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds annually.

The parents of Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023, welcomed the announcement.

The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to Parliamentary approval.

Students Barnaby and Grace, and caretaker Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.

Barnaby's mother, Emma Webber, said: "This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do.

"It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers' money.

"A hospital bed does not erase the egregious crimes committed, nor the destruction they have caused.

"Closing this loophole finally delivers some basic accountability that victims deserve."

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.

"Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount.

"On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.

"On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated."

The mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche who was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape in Hackney, east London, in April 2024, also lobbied for benefits paid to offenders in psychiatric hospitals to stop.

Tape was given a hospital order detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.

Kennedi's mother Linda Westcarr said: "For many victims' families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.

"In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised."

The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise.

"For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

"That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."

Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.

"Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.

"The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."

The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983 and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.

The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.

Murder is not included because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.

The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impacts of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.
